questiontext.text:
Goal

A juice bar recipe lists each blend and its sugar count. During detox week, the printer needs only the low-sugar blends, and the board displays every sugar count at half its original value.

Read
  • For statements with range clause. Find the table row for an array or slice. What does each iteration-value column contain? What is the type of each value?
  • Compare the opening sentence with the table's second value column. How does an iteration value reach its variable? What does that assignment do to a struct value?
  • Find the paragraph beginning "For an array, pointer to array, or slice value a". According to its last sentence, how many times does a nil slice iterate?
Coming from Java

The reflex is a stream chain, one stage per verb, with a null guard in front because a for-each over null throws. The second reflex is writing through the loop variable.

return board.stream()
        .filter(b -> b.sugar() < limit)
        .map(Blend::slug)
        .toList();
Banned: slices. Required: range
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • The table gives a slice two columns of iteration values, so decide which column halve must write through.
  • Search the section for the word nil and read the sentence around it, then decide what clean(nil, 5) returns.

testcode.text: board := []blend{{"Kale Cooler", 4}, {"Mango Rush", 9}} fmt.Println(clean(board, 5)) fmt.Println(board) halve(board) fmt.Println(board)

board := []blend{{"Kale Cooler", 5}, {"Mango Rush", 9}, {"Celery Tonic", 2}} fmt.Println(clean(board, 5)) halve(board) fmt.Println(board) fmt.Println(clean(board, 4)) fmt.Println(clean(nil, 5), len(clean([]blend{}, 5))) halve(nil)

questiontext.text:
Goal

After the last match, an announcer counts players off the field one at a time, from the highest number down to 1. The big screen stops the count as soon as it has enough names. The screen shows the first number under the floor it was given, and it shows 0 when no player is under the floor. When nobody is on the field, the announcer counts nobody off.

Read
  • iter.Seq. Read the type line and its two sentences. What does the iterator pass to yield? What does yield return? When must the iterator stop early?
  • iter, the Iterators section near the top. Which two events stop an iterator? What happens if it calls yield again?
Coming from Java

The reflex is an Iterator with hasNext and next, where the consumer holds the loop and pulls each element. Go puts the loop on the other side, and the linked page says which side that is. The other reflex is building the whole sequence up front and handing back a list.

Iterator<Integer> it = countdown(5);
while (it.hasNext()) {
    process(it.next());
}
Banned: append, make
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Search the iter overview for the word panics and read the sentence around it.
  • The same Iterators section has one worked iterator further down, so read the two lines inside its loop before you write your own.

Goal

The stadium's lost property office has a bin of items but no inventory. Staff need the labels in ascending order and the total number of items, duplicates included. They also need to visit the labels handed in more than a given number of times without receiving the full list. over hands out those labels in the same ascending order as labels and stops as soon as the caller stops.

Read
  • maps.Keys. Read the signature and both sentences. What type does it return? In what order does it produce keys?
  • slices.Collect. Read both sentences. What argument does it accept? What does it return for an empty sequence?
  • slices.Sort. Read the first sentence and signature. Which slice is sorted? What does the call return?
Coming from Java

The reflex is keySet, which hands back a collection with a size that you can walk twice. The second reflex is trusting the order the map hands you, an order Java's own HashMap never promised either. Read the return type on each linked page before you assume any of the three is a list.

List<String> labels = new ArrayList<>(counts.keySet());
Collections.sort(labels);
Required: slices.Collect, maps.Keys
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Of the three maps entries that hand back a sequence, pick the one whose values are the map's keys.
  • Reread slices.Collect for an empty bin, then the iter overview's Iterators section for what over owes a stopping caller.

testcode.text: b := newBin() b.hand("scarf") b.hand("boot") b.hand("scarf") fmt.Println(b.labels(), b.total())
b := newBin() b.hand("glove") b.hand("glove") b.hand("hat") for label := range b.over(1) { fmt.Println(label) }

expected.text: [anorak boot kite scarf whistle] 8 anorak boot 2

questiontext.text:
Goal

A costume hire shop asks its program for prices from a list of costumes. An AI returned Go code that imitates a Java stream. Every test passes, but each enquiry copies the full list before reading one price.

Read
  • slices.DeleteFunc. Read all three sentences. Which slice does it modify? What remains beyond the new length?
  • slices.Clone. Read all four sentences. What does Clone return? Why does the AI call it before DeleteFunc?
  • slices, the Index near the top. Is there an entry that converts every element to a different type? What does the answer tell you about where to write the conversion?
Coming from Java

The reflex is a stream chain, where each stage hands a fresh collection to the next and no stage touches the source. The AI's code keeps that shape, one named helper per verb, so it reads as familiar and safe. Check each of those calls against the linked docs before you trust the resemblance.

return list.stream()
        .filter(h -> h.cost() <= budget)
        .map(Hire::costume)
        .sorted()
        .toList();
Banned: slices.Clone, slices.DeleteFunc
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Count how many times the AI's affordable walks the list, then write down the smallest number of walks the job needs.
  • Read the DeleteFunc sentence about elements past the new length, then say why the AI calls Clone first.
